analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax deduction for employer campaigns against union organizing.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 137 House members (all Democrats), has sat without action in the House Ways and Means Committee since its April 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, companies can deduct as a business expense what they spend on consultants, lawyers, and captive-audience meetings to persuade employees against forming a union. This bill would end that deduction, require employers and the outside consultants they hire to report such spending to the IRS, and fine employers that fail to report. It would also make nondeductible the costs connected to actions that lead to a federal unfair-labor-practice charge or settlement.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to join or form a union. Today a company can treat its anti-union campaign as an ordinary business cost, with other taxpayers effectively picking up part of the bill; the bill removes that subsidy and forces the spending into the open, so employees would face employer persuasion campaigns that the employer alone pays for and that are publicly reported.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds anti-union spending to the list of nondeductible expenses in Section 162 of the tax code, which already denies deductions for lobbying and political campaign spending, extending the same principle to employer campaigns aimed at employees' union decisions.

The bill counts as nondeductible the cost of any meeting or training where labor organizations are discussed, and the cost of actions that result in an unfair-labor-practice complaint, a related settlement, or a finding of coercion under the Railway Labor Act.

Employers would have to file an information return describing these activities and amounts, with penalties of the greater of $10,000 or $1,000 per full-time employee, and higher penalties if noncompliance continues; outside consultants who run such campaigns would also have to report.

The bill's findings cite Economic Policy Institute research that companies spend about $340 million a year on consultants to sway workers' views on unions and that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in roughly 4 of 10 union elections in 2016-2017.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that run campaigns against union organizing would lose the tax deduction for those costs, and outside union-avoidance consultants and the law and HR firms that support such campaigns would face new disclosure requirements and reduced demand for their services.

drawbacks.text: The definition of covered spending is broad: any meeting or training where a labor organization is merely discussed becomes nondeductible, which could sweep in routine HR meetings and compliance trainings and force companies into costly line-item accounting to separate those costs from ordinary wages.

Deduction disallowance can be triggered retroactively: costs become nondeductible if an action later results in an NLRB complaint or settlement, so a company could lose a deduction years after the fact over a charge, though costs tied to a complaint that is fully set aside are excluded.

The paperwork penalty is the greater of $10,000 or $1,000 per full-time employee, which for a large employer could reach tens of millions of dollars for a filing failure, though the penalty for continued failure after notice is capped at $100,000 and penalties can be waived for reasonable cause.

Business interests would argue the tax code is the wrong tool for labor policy and that employers have a legitimate right to communicate with their own employees; the bill responds by carving out direct bargaining, voluntary recognition, and legally required postings, but the line-drawing would fall to Treasury regulations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is targeted and mirrors a principle already in the tax code for political spending: lawful but taxpayer-subsidized influence operations lose the deduction. The carve-outs for normal bargaining and voluntary recognition limit the blast radius. The real risks are compliance cost and over-breadth in what counts as a 'meeting where labor organizations are discussed,' and the per-employee penalty structure is steep; on balance the bill is a straightforward subsidy removal whose main costs fall on employers that run anti-union campaigns.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 7, 2025, and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means; the action record shows no further steps, no markup, and no vote.
137 House members — the sponsor plus 136 cosponsors — are attached to the bill, all of them Democrats, and none of the chamber's 223 Republicans have cosponsored it.
With Republicans holding a House majority of 223 to 217 and chairing Ways and Means, the committee has not scheduled the bill, so it has never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and union-avoidance consultants keep the tax deduction for anti-union spending and face no new disclosure, while workers remain subject to employer-funded persuasion campaigns. Nothing has been resolved; the bill could still move if the committee acts.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no markup, hearing, or floor scheduling — since its referral on April 7, 2025.

against.name: 223 of 223 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled committee to which it was referred has not advanced it.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat (137 of the chamber's 217 Democrats), no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee has not acted.

industries.note: These firms, which bill employers roughly $340 million a year to steer workers away from unions, would see the tax deductibility of their services end and would themselves face new IRS reporting, cutting both demand and anonymity.

industries.industry: Employers that campaign against union organizing
industries.note: They would lose the deduction for anti-union spending, including wages and costs tied to captive-audience meetings and to actions that draw unfair-labor-practice complaints, and would owe new filings and penalties.
Removing the taxpayer subsidy for employer counter-campaigns would tilt union elections toward workers' own choices, the outcome the bill's findings say federal labor policy is meant to encourage.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the House Ways and Means Committee usually die there without a markup unless the committee chair schedules one, and this bill has seen no action in months with no Republican support. Its most likely path is expiring at the end of this Congress without a vote, with a chance of reintroduction if House control or committee leadership changes.
